summary.text: The universal quantifier also includes \(n=0\); with the divisor sums and totient at zero equal to \(0\), the defining expression gives \(a(0)=0\), although \(0\) is neither \(1\) nor prime.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 a(n)=\Bigl(\sigma_2(n)+\varphi(n)\sigma(n)-2n^2\Bigr)_{\ge 0},
\]
where \(\sigma(n)\) is the sum of the divisors used in the definition, \(\sigma_2(n)\) is the sum of their squares, and \((x)_{\ge 0}=\max(x,0)\) denotes conversion of the integer expression back to a natural number. For positive \(n\), this is the expression in A072780 whenever the integer inside the parentheses is nonnegative.

The formal statement under consideration quantifies over every natural number \(n\), rather than only over \(n\ge 1\). We disprove that formal statement by taking
\[
n=0.
\]

First compute \(a(0)\) under the conventions in its definition. The finite divisor set used for a natural number \(n\) consists of the integers \(d\) satisfying
\[
1\le d<n+1\qquad\text{and}\qquad d\mid n.
\]
For \(n=0\), the inequalities would be \(1\le d<1\), which no natural number satisfies. Thus the finite divisor set of \(0\) used here is empty. Consequently, both relevant divisor sums are empty sums and hence equal to zero:
\[
\sigma(0)=\sum_{d\mid 0}d=0,
\qquad
\sigma_2(0)=\sum_{d\mid 0}d^2=0.
\]
Here the displayed sums are understood with precisely the finite-divisor-set convention just described; they are not sums over all positive integers dividing zero.

Likewise, the totient at zero is zero under the natural-number convention used in the definition. Indeed, \(\varphi(n)\) counts the natural numbers \(r<n\) that are coprime to \(n\). There is no natural number \(r<0\), so the set counted by \(\varphi(0)\) is empty and
\[
\varphi(0)=0.
\]
Also, \(0^2=0\). Substitution therefore gives
\[
\sigma_2(0)+\varphi(0)\sigma(0)-2\cdot0^2
 =0+0\cdot0-0
 =0.
\]
Taking the nonnegative natural part of zero still gives zero, so
\[
a(0)=0.
\]

Now consider the claimed characterization of the zero values:
\[
a(n)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad n=1\ \text{or}\ n\text{ is prime}.
\]
At \(n=0\), its left-hand side is true by the computation above. Its right-hand side is false. Certainly \(0\ne1\). Moreover, \(0\) is not prime: every prime natural number is at least \(2\), whereas \(0<2\).

Equivalently, if one assumes the universally quantified characterization and specializes it to \(n=0\), then from \(a(0)=0\) one obtains the disjunction
\[
0=1\quad\text{or}\quad 0\text{ is prime}.
\]
There are two cases. The first case contradicts \(0\ne1\), and the second contradicts the fact that zero is not prime. Thus both alternatives are impossible, giving a contradiction.

The full formal conjecture is a conjunction of this zero-value characterization with the additional assertion
\[
a(n)=2\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
n=pq\text{ for two distinct primes }p,q.
\]
A conjunction can hold universally only if its first component holds universally. Since the first component already fails at \(n=0\), no analysis of the second component is needed. Hence the universally quantified statement over all natural numbers is false.

This counterexample depends entirely on the inclusion of \(0\) in the quantifier. The OEIS conjecture as canonically stated ranges only over \(n\ge1\). Therefore \(n=0\) is not a counterexample to that positive-integer conjecture; it disproves the accepted formal version, which omitted the hypothesis \(n\ge1\).
